restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the SmPCs or MHRA pages accessed.

items.t: Adults (including elderly) and children over 16 years: 1 g (two 500 mg tablets) every 4 hours as required. Maximum 8 tablets (4 g) in 24 hours; no more than 4 doses in 24 hours. Do not take for more than 3 days without consulting a doctor.

src.q: Adults, Elderly and Children over 16 years: Two tablets every four hours as required. Not more than eight tablets in 24 hours
nor should more than four doses be given in any 24 hour period
Do not take for more than 3 days without consulting your doctor.

items.t: 250 mg/5 mL suspension, adults and children over 16 years: 10-20 mL (500 mg-1 g) up to 4 times a day.

src.q: Adults and children over 16 years: Two - four 5mL spoonfuls (large end) up to 4 times a day.

items.t: Elderly: absorption is normal but half-life is longer and clearance lower than in young adults (no specific dose change stated).

src.q: In the elderly, the rate and extent of paracetamol absorption is normal but plasma half-life is longer and paracetamol clearance is lower than in young adults.

items.t: Low body weight or hepatic risk factors: no reduced maximum daily dose is stated in the oral SmPCs used (BNF not accessed); this is a gap in these sources, not evidence that no reduction is needed. Overdose thresholds stated: liver damage is possible after 10 g or more in adults (500 mg tablet SmPC) or 7.5 g or more in adults and adolescents aged 12 years and over (suspension SmPCs), and after 5 g or more with risk factors (long-term liver enzyme inducers, regular excess alcohol, glutathione depletion e.g. eating disorders, cystic fibrosis, HIV, starvation, cachexia).

src.q: Liver damage is possible in adults who have taken 10g or more of paracetamol. Ingestion of 5g or more of paracetamol may lead to liver damage if the patient has risk factors
Liver damage is possible in adults and adolescents (≥12 years of age) who have taken 7.5g or more of paracetamol.
is likely to be glutathione deplete e.g. eating disorders, cystic fibrosis, HIV infection, starvation, cachexia

items.t: Tablets: not recommended under 10 years. Children 10-15 years: one 500 mg tablet every 4-6 hours when necessary, maximum 4 doses in 24 hours; no more than 3 days without a doctor.

src.q: Children under 10 years: Not recommended for children under 10 years of age.
Children aged 10 to 15 years: One tablet every four to six hours when necessary to a maximum of four doses in 24 hours.

items.t: 120 mg/5 ml, fever after vaccination at 2, 3 and 4 months: 2.5 ml, up to 4 times a day starting at the time of vaccination, at least 4 hours apart; see a doctor or pharmacist if still needed 2 days after the vaccine.

src.q: For the relief of fever after vaccinations at 2, 3 and 4 months 2.5ml. This dose may be given up to 4 times a day starting at the time of vaccination.
If your baby still needs this medicine two days after receiving the vaccine talk to your doctor or pharmacist.

items.t: MHRA 2011 table (older): post-vaccination fever at 2-3 months 2.5 mL, then a second 2.5 mL after 4-6 hours if necessary; no more than 2 doses. This differs from the current 120 mg/5 ml suspension SmPC (up to 4 doses a day).

src.q: Post-vaccination fever 2.5 mL If necessary, after 4-6 hours, give a second 2.5 mL dose
Do not give more than 2 doses.

src.q: Pain and other causes of fever - if your baby weighs over 4 kg and was born after 37 weeks 2.5 ml If necessary, after 4-6 hours, give a second 2.5 ml dose
Do not give to babies less than 2 months of age. Leave at least 4 hours between doses. Do not give more than 2 doses.

items.t: High anion gap metabolic acidosis (pyroglutamic acidosis) reported with prolonged therapeutic use in severe illness (e.g. severe renal impairment, sepsis), malnutrition or chronic alcoholism, or with flucloxacillin. If suspected, stop paracetamol promptly and monitor closely.

src.q: Cases of high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) due to pyroglutamic acidosis have been reported in patients with severe illness such as severe renal impairment and sepsis
If HAGMA due to pyroglutamic acidosis is suspected, prompt discontinuation of paracetamol and close monitoring is recommended.

items.t: Can be used in pregnancy if clinically needed, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and lowest frequency. Large amount of data shows no malformative or feto/neonatal toxicity.

items.t: MHRA (2025): paracetamol is the first-choice pain reliever in pregnancy; no evidence it causes autism. Patients should not swap to ibuprofen (NSAIDs generally not recommended in pregnancy).

src.q: paracetamol is recommended as the first-choice pain reliever for pregnant women, used at the lowest dose and for the shortest duration

patients should not swap to alternatives such as ibuprofen
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, are generally not recommended during pregnancy

items.t: BUMPS: can be used throughout pregnancy for pain and fever; no extra monitoring needed.
